transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. Thank you for coming in today. What brings you to the clinic?

Hi, Doctor. Thanks for seeing me. 

Um, I guess the main reason I’m here is that I'm really struggling with certain parts of my job. I manage health services, and anything that takes real, sitting-down brain work... it just feels like I hit a wall. 

Things like putting together the monthly reports or trying to plan out a multi-site health event, I just keep putting them off. Even when I know how much it matters and that people are waiting on it, I just avoid doing it. It's starting to become a real problem.
When you're avoiding these work tasks, do you find yourself feeling anxious or worried about them, or is it more that you just can't seem to focus and get started on them?

I'm not really sure if anxiety is the right word. I mean, I guess I get a little stressed when I know people are waiting on me and the deadline is right there, but... mostly it's just that I can't get going. 

I'll sit down at my desk to do the report, open up the file, and my brain just sort of... refuses to engage with it. It's like I just can't seem to focus enough to actually take that first step and start the work.

When you're sitting at your desk trying to start these reports, do unwanted thoughts or worries keep popping into your head and making it hard to concentrate, or is it more that your mind just feels blank or wandering?

It's definitely not worries or unwanted thoughts like that. It's more that my mind just wanders, or I get pulled away by every little thing. 

It's not just at my desk, either. Like, I’ll be in a meeting trying to listen to a budget update, and... if a phone vibrates, or I hear people talking out in the hall, I completely lose my focus. Even just a random thought popping into my head, like remembering something I forgot to do for the league, will just pull me right away. Next thing I know, I tune back in and realize I've completely missed the last few minutes of what was said. So yeah, it's not anxiety, my brain just easily drifts off.
Have you always struggled with focusing and getting distracted easily, even back when you were in school or earlier in your career? Or is this something that's more recently become a problem for you?

No, it's definitely not a new thing. I've pretty much always been like this. 

Um, even way back in elementary school, my teachers used to tell my parents that I was a bright kid, but that I was just always daydreaming. I was constantly losing my worksheets, and I'd always forget to actually turn in my homework. Honestly, the only way anything ever got handed in was because my mom would check my backpack every single night to make sure it was there. So... yeah, it's been a struggle for as long as I can remember.

When you're trying to sit down and focus on work, do you find yourself feeling restless or fidgety, like you need to move around or get up from your desk? Or do you stay physically still but just mentally drift off?

I don't really feel restless, no. I mean, I'm not bouncing my leg or feeling like I have to get up and pace around the office or anything like that. I usually just sit there at my desk. It's really just the mental part. I stay perfectly still, but my brain is just... off somewhere else.

You mentioned you don't feel restless or fidgety at your desk, but I'm curious—in other situations, do you find yourself acting or speaking without thinking things through first? For example, do you interrupt people, make quick decisions you later regret, or do things impulsively?

No, not really. I don't think I struggle with that. I'm not really one to interrupt people... honestly, I'm usually just trying to catch up on what they were saying because I spaced out. And I don't really make rash decisions or do things impulsively, either. If anything, I probably take too long to get things done. So, no, I wouldn't say I act or speak without thinking.

Beyond work, do you find that this difficulty with focus and getting distracted is also causing problems in other areas of your life—like at home, in your personal relationships, or with managing household responsibilities?

Yeah, it definitely spills over. I mean, I'm still getting by overall, both at work and in the community, but... it's not without problems. 

People end up having to cover gaps for me when I drop the ball, and I've had deadlines slip. And it definitely affects my personal life, too. I've embarrassed myself more times than I can count having to make these frantic, last-minute apologies to friends—just like I do with my coworkers—because I forgot something we planned or just completely lost track of time. So yeah, it's definitely not just a work thing.

You mentioned you don't feel restless at your desk, but I'm wondering—in your daily life overall, do you find yourself having a lot of excess energy? For instance, do you tend to be very active, exercise a lot, or find it hard to sit still for extended periods in general, like during movies, long car rides, or social gatherings?

No, I wouldn't say I have excess energy. I'm not overly active or anything like that. I don't have a problem sitting through a movie or a long car ride. Like I said before, I'm not really a fidgety person. It's more of a mental thing for me rather than a physical need to move around.

You mentioned that people have had to cover gaps for you at work and you've missed some deadlines. How much would you say this has affected your ability to keep your job or advance in your career? Has anyone ever suggested you might lose your position because of these issues?

Well, it hasn't come to that. I've never been threatened with losing my job or anything. I mean, I'm a manager, so I have a certain level of responsibility, and I do manage to get the important things done eventually. It's just... it takes a lot more effort than it probably should, and I rely on my team a bit too much to catch the things I miss. As for advancing... I don't know. I suppose it might be holding me back from moving up further, just because I'm not always seen as the most organized or reliable person when it comes to the details. But no one has ever told me my job is on the line.

On a scale of 1 to 10, how much distress or frustration does this difficulty with focus and attention cause you in your daily life? And how much would you say it's interfering with your ability to do what you want to do?

I'd probably put it at... maybe a 6 or a 7 out of 10 for frustration. 

I mean, like I mentioned earlier, I am still getting by—both at work and just out in the community. I'm functioning. But it definitely interferes enough to be a real problem. It's just really frustrating knowing that other people are having to cover gaps for me, or watching deadlines slip when I know I should have handled them better. 

And honestly, the embarrassment of having to constantly make those last-minute apologies to my coworkers and my friends... it takes a toll on you. So, it doesn't completely stop me from doing what I need to do, but it just makes everything a lot harder and more stressful than it should be.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a lifelong history of inattention, easy distractibility, and difficulty with sustained focus that began in elementary school and persists into adulthood. Core symptoms include: mind wandering during meetings, difficulty initiating complex tasks, forgetfulness, and chronic disorganization. Notably absent are hyperactivity, restlessness, fidgetiness, and impulsive behaviors. The symptoms cause moderate functional impairment across multiple domains (work, social, personal relationships) with distress rated 6-7/10. The clinical presentation is consistent with Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder, Predominantly Inattentive Type (F90.0), but given the absence of documented hyperactivity symptoms and the patient's explicit denial of excess energy or physical restlessness, F90.9 (ADHD, unspecified type) is most appropriate as the primary diagnosis.
